documents.title: Generative AI Guidance
documents.summary: IT Services guidance on using and procuring generative AI tools, mostly on data protection, accuracy and ownership of output, tool review and procurement. It sets no student-facing stance on AI in coursework and sends academic-integrity questions to the teaching center and the Student Manual.
documents.stance_why: The page never says whether students may use AI in coursework. The one academic-integrity item says only 'it is recommended that instructors contact the Chicago Center for Teaching and Learning', so the decision is left to instructors and the teaching center; the binding rules concern confidential data and tool review.

units.why: The opening says members 'must consider issues related to information security, privacy, compliance, and academic integrity', a duty to weigh four issue areas; it frames the scope and principles of the guidance rather than one use, so P56, must, general.
units.anchor: must consider issues related to information security, privacy, compliance, and academic integrity
units.resolution_why: A coded modality informs, B coded must. The source says members 'must consider issues related to information security, privacy, compliance, and academic integrity', an explicit duty, so must; type P56 (both agree) because it frames scope and principles rather than a specific rule.

units.why: The text says tools 'offer many capabilities and efficiencies that can greatly enhance our work', naming a benefit with no rule attached, so P87, informs, neutral.
units.anchor: Generative AI tools offer many capabilities and efficiencies that can greatly enhance our work
units.resolution_why: A coded unit_stance neutral, B encourage. The sentence only states that tools 'offer many capabilities and efficiencies that can greatly enhance our work' and recommends nothing, so neutral; P87 and informs agreed.

units.why: 'Is prohibited without prior security and privacy review' bans confidential data in public tools unless reviewed, so P50 (protect confidential data), must-not, restrict; it binds everyone in the community.
units.anchor: confidential data with publicly available generative AI tools is prohibited

units.why: The sentence lists what counts as confidential (employee data, FERPA student data, HIPAA data, unpublished research), defining the scope of the data rule, so P50 informs rather than a new rule.
units.anchor: personally identifiable employee data, FERPA-covered student data, HIPAA-covered patient data
units.fit_note: Defines which data counts as confidential; not itself a protect-data rule.

units.why: It says some grantors 'have policies prohibiting the use of generative AI tools in analyzing or reviewing grant applications', pointing to funder rules on research and grant review, which is P62 and informs.
units.anchor: policies prohibiting the use of generative AI tools in analyzing or reviewing grant applications

units.why: It warns that shared information 'may expose sensitive information to unauthorized parties or violate data use agreements', a reason for protecting data, so P50 informs.
units.anchor: may expose sensitive information to unauthorized parties or violate data use agreements

units.why: The text refers readers to Policy 601 for definitions of confidential data, tying the guidance to an existing university policy (P77), so informs.
units.anchor: Please see Policy 601 or definitions of confidential data and its use for more information.
units.fit_note: Cross-reference to Policy 601 for definitions rather than a rule that AI use must comply.
units.resolution_why: Only coder A found this unit. The source says 'Please see Policy 601 or definitions of confidential data and its use', a real cross-reference to an existing university policy, so kept as P77 informs.

units.why: 'AI-generated content may be misleading or inaccurate' and may cite content that 'does not exist' is a warning about output reliability, so P31, informs, general.
units.anchor: Generative AI technology may create citations to content that does not exist.
units.resolution_why: A coded phase during-work, B general. The sentences are warnings about the nature of AI output ('may be misleading or inaccurate'; 'may create citations to content that does not exist') and are not tied to a work step, so general.

units.why: 'may contain content and materials from other authors and may be copyrighted' is a general copyright fact about AI output, so P52, informs, general.
units.anchor: may contain content and materials from other authors and may be copyrighted
units.resolution_why: A coded phase during-work, B general. 'may contain content and materials from other authors and may be copyrighted' is a general fact about AI output, not an instruction for a work step, so general.

units.why: 'It is the responsibility of the tool user to review the accuracy and ownership of any AI-generated content' puts a duty on the user to verify output, so P31 must; it also names ownership, hence the fit_note. It does not require AI use, so unit_stance neutral. P29 (own submitted work) does not fit.
units.anchor: responsibility of the tool user to review the accuracy and ownership of any AI-generated content.
units.fit_note: Also makes the user responsible for checking ownership (copyright) of AI output, not only accuracy. Also requires review of ownership (copyright) of AI-generated content, not only accuracy.
units.resolution_why: A coded unit_stance require, B neutral. 'It is the responsibility of the tool user to review the accuracy and ownership of any AI-generated content' assigns a duty to check output but does not require AI use, so neutral. P31 with fit_note retained since ownership is also named.

units.why: It recommends that instructors contact the teaching center on academic honesty and AI, deferring the academic-integrity rule to that unit and instructors; best fit is P63 (support faculty), not P04 since no instructor-level rule is stated.
units.anchor: it is recommended that instructors contact the Chicago Center for Teaching and Learning
units.fit_note: The document sets no integrity rule itself and only sends instructors to the teaching center. Also: Also defers the whole academic-integrity question to the teaching center; the page sets no integrity rule itself.

units.why: It points to 'Academic Honesty & Plagiarism in the Student Manual for University policy' as the governing integrity rule, an existing policy that applies (P77), informs, general.
units.anchor: Academic Honesty & Plagiarism in the Student Manual for University policy
units.fit_note: Points to existing academic-honesty policy without saying AI misuse falls under it.
units.resolution_why: Only coder A found this unit; B did not. The sentence '(See Academic Honesty & Plagiarism in the Student Manual for University policy.)' points to an existing policy, which is real policy content. A coded when-misuse; the pointer does not describe misuse handling itself, so phase general. P77 with fit_note retained.

units.why: 'require a security review before they are acquired, even if the software is free' is a mandatory pre-acquisition review for AI tools that handle confidential data, so P65, must; it binds anyone acquiring such tools, hence actor all.
units.anchor: require a security review before they are acquired, even if the software is free
units.resolution_why: A coded actor all, B admin. The sentence says AI products that handle confidential data 'require a security review before they are acquired'; whoever acquires them is bound, and the page addresses the whole University community, so all.

units.why: It tells people to submit the review form 'before acquiring or using any tools, add-ons, or modules' with generative AI and confidential data, a review-and-approval duty (P65), must.
units.anchor: before acquiring or using any tools, add-ons, or modules

units.why: Members who wish to use a tool 'should first review the approved tools and use cases', so they should use the approved list (P92), should; it answers whether use is permitted and does not ban unlisted tools, so unit_stance permit.
units.anchor: should first review the approved tools and use cases
units.resolution_why: A coded unit_stance permit, B restrict. The FAQ answers whether AI use for University work is permitted by saying users 'should first review the approved tools and use cases'; it does not ban unlisted tools (next entries give a review route for them), so permit with a check step.

units.why: The site is 'updated bi-monthly with decisions approved by' the CTO and CISO, naming who decides on approved tools and how often, so P80, informs, over-time; P54 does not fit since it concerns the tool list, not the policy.
units.anchor: updated bi-monthly with decisions approved by the University
units.fit_note: Also implies a recurring update cycle of the approved-tools list.
units.resolution_why: A coded phase over-time, B general. The list is 'updated bi-monthly with decisions approved by' the CTO and CISO, so the sentence states a recurring update cycle as well as who decides; over-time kept, with the fit_note on the update cycle.

units.why: For a tool not on the list, paid tools go through ServiceNow Procurement Intake, a review-and-approval process (P65), should.
units.anchor: For paid tools, individuals should submit a request through ServiceNow Procurement Intake.
units.fit_note: Splits the route by paid versus free tools.

units.why: 'For free tools, individuals should submit the Generative AI Tool Evaluation Form' is the matching rule for free tools, P65, should. Distinct from the paid-tool route so kept separate.
units.anchor: For free tools, individuals should submit the Generative AI Tool Evaluation Form.
units.resolution_why: Only coder A found this unit; B merged paid and free routes into one unit. The source gives two separate rules ('For paid tools ... ServiceNow Procurement Intake'; 'For free tools ... Generative AI Tool Evaluation Form'), so kept as a separate unit.

units.why: The forms "inform updates to the University's approved tools and use cases list", describing how the list is revised, so P54 is the nearest type but fits only partly.
units.anchor: helps inform updates to the University's approved tools and use cases list
units.fit_note: About updating the approved-tool list from review requests, not the whole policy.
units.resolution_why: Only coder B found this unit. The source says completing the review forms 'helps inform updates to the University's approved tools and use cases list', a real statement about how the list is revised. P54 (revisit regularly) fits only partly since it concerns the tool list, not the whole policy; fit_note kept.

units.why: Researchers using AI in human-subjects studies 'must inform the Institutional Review Board', a rule for AI in research (P62), must.
units.anchor: must inform the Institutional Review Board

units.why: 'The IRB must be aware of any technology used to collect, process, or analyze human subjects data' sets an oversight duty on research AI, P62; separate from the researcher's duty so kept as its own unit.
units.anchor: must be aware of any technology used to collect, process, or analyze human subjects data
units.resolution_why: Only coder A found this unit. 'The IRB must be aware of any technology used to collect, process, or analyze human subjects data' is a separate oversight duty from the researchers' duty to inform the IRB, so kept as P62.

units.why: The review purpose is to 'prevent inadvertent exposure of institutional data to external systems', explaining why tool review exists, so P65 informs.
units.anchor: prevent inadvertent exposure of institutional data to external systems

units.why: Reviews weigh research and compliance obligations, system impact, requester context, safeguards and business case: criteria for approving AI tools, P65, informs.
units.anchor: Information Assurance reviews generative AI tools to ensure they are used securely, responsibly

units.why: 'Use of University data by vendors to train or improve their models is not permitted' limits what AI providers may do with University data and is applied in review, so P65, must-not, prohibit; actor admin since the University applies it to vendors.
units.anchor: Use of University data by vendors to train or improve their models is not permitted.
units.resolution_why: A coded actor all, B admin. 'Use of University data by vendors to train or improve their models is not permitted' is a review criterion applied by the University (Information Assurance) to vendors, not a rule for community members, so admin.

units.why: 'Requests involving elevated or unresolved risk are escalated to senior leadership for final determination' names who decides hard cases, so P80, informs, general.
units.anchor: Requests involving elevated or unresolved risk are escalated to senior leadership for final determination.
units.resolution_why: A coded phase before-course, B general. Escalation of 'elevated or unresolved risk' to senior leadership is a standing decision procedure not tied to a course phase, so general.

units.why: It suggests evaluating PhoenixAI, the university's internal platform, when a tool fails review; this is an institution-wide provided tool, so P92 (not P17, which is course-specific), may.
units.anchor: The University's internal generative AI platform may now provide equivalent functionality.
units.fit_note: Offers PhoenixAI as an alternative to unapproved tools rather than requiring approved tools.

units.why: It says to select an alternative from the approved list when a tool fails review, so use approved tools (P92), should.
units.anchor: Approved options are listed at genai.uchicago.edu/generative-ai-tools.
units.resolution_why: Only coder A found this unit. 'Approved options are listed at genai.uchicago.edu/generative-ai-tools' is the instruction to pick an approved alternative when a tool fails review, a distinct rule from the PhoenixAI suggestion, so kept as P92.

units.why: A Risk Acceptance Letter is 'formal acknowledgment' that leadership accepts defined risks, the process for granting an exception to the review standard, so P80, informs, general.
units.anchor: Getting an exception through a Risk Acceptance Letter (RAL)
units.resolution_why: A coded phase before-course, B general. The Risk Acceptance Letter exception route is a standing procedure, not tied to course set-up, so general.

units.why: Paid or enterprise versions 'are often required because they provide enhanced security', a justification for preferring vetted licensed tools, P50.
units.anchor: Paid or enterprise versions of AI tools are often required because they provide enhanced security

units.why: Contract review lets the university attach AI, privacy, security and IP terms to purchased tools (P65), informs.
units.anchor: attach or negotiate AI, privacy, security, and intellectual property terms.

units.why: 'The tool must be purchased through Procurement' when free protections are insufficient, a purchasing approval rule (P65), must.
units.anchor: purchased through Procurement

units.why: The enterprise route means 'the University already has an institutional agreement in place', i.e. licensed tools with set terms, so P92 informs.
units.anchor: the University already has an institutional agreement in place
units.resolution_why: Only coder A found this unit. The source defines enterprise versions as the University already having 'an institutional agreement in place' that sets terms of use, which is a statement about licensed tools (P92 informs); kept though low-weight.

units.why: The stated goal is that 'the University community benefits from AI innovation while maintaining compliance', a purpose statement for the framework, P56.
units.anchor: the University community benefits from AI innovation while maintaining compliance

notes: Single IT-security guidance document, no academic-integrity rule of its own. The Provost AI and Education Working Group report and the faculty/CCTL pages were inaccessible or not included per collect notes. The contacts line ('If you have questions about the guidelines, please contact') was dropped as navigation.
